title: DFS on Chicago: Real Map Intersections ⚡
description: Watch Depth-First Search (DFS) walk street intersections like a stack-driven explorer—one branch deep, then backtrack. In this visualization, you’ll see how DFS traversal differs from “shortest path” thinking and why route results can vary.
ig_caption:
Depth First Search (DFS) Traversal on Real Street Maps… what happens when DFS explores real city intersections ⚡ First, we model streets as a graph: intersections = nodes, roads = edges. Then DFS uses a stack/recursion to go as deep as possible along one route before backtracking—so the “visited” pattern is deterministic by neighbor order.

Key mechanics (what you’re seeing in the reel):
1) Mark node visited (prevents cycles)
2) Pick next neighbor (ordering changes traversal)
3) Keep diving deep until dead-end
4) Backtrack and continue until the component is fully explored

Takeaway: DFS is a graph traversal strategy (great for reachability/structure), not a guaranteed shortest-path algorithm.

Debate question: If we reorder neighbors (e.g., N/E/S/W preference), should the “best-looking” DFS route change?
